guard.G1.brief: Someone is at the warehouse door saying a password. Let in only people whose password matches exactly, and block everyone else.
guard.G1.concept: Authentication: only let in people who are verified
guard.G1.crowIntro: I bet I can guess one little warehouse key~
guard.G1.crowLose: One letter off and it won't open? So picky!
guard.G1.ria: Please guard the warehouse door. Open it only when the password is right.
guard.G1.title: Warehouse Door Password
guard.G1.why.0: It matches the password exactly, so let it in.
guard.G1.why.1: Even one capital letter makes it a different password.
guard.G1.why.2: A space in the middle makes it a different password.
guard.G1.why.3: That is just a guess with an easy number, so block it.
guard.G1.why.4: The right password gets in every time.
guard.G1.why.5: That is just the word "password", not the password.
guard.G1.why.6: An empty value should be blocked too.
guard.G1.why.7: Extra characters after the password make it a different password. A matching beginning is not enough.
guard.G1.why.8: A leading space makes it a different password. Do not quietly trim it away.
guard.G10.brief: This time count only wrong tries in a row. When the right password is given, reset the fail count to 0. After 3 wrong tries in a row, lock it and block everything, even the right password.
guard.G10.concept: Lockout after consecutive failures (an attacker may lock real users out on purpose, so in practice time-based lockouts and extra checks are used too)
guard.G10.crowIntro: Wrong, right, wrong... I'll mix up my knocks~
guard.G10.crowLose: Three in a row? So I get a pass if I rest once?
guard.G10.ria: Success clears the fail count. Lock only after 3 wrong tries in a row.
guard.G10.title: The Lock That Counts Only Streaks
guard.G10.why.0: The password is right, so let it in.
guard.G10.why.1: A typo, so block it. The streak of failures is now 1.
guard.G10.why.10: It is locked, so block it even though the password is right.
guard.G10.why.2: Wrong again, so block it. The streak is now 2.
guard.G10.why.3: Right, so let it in and reset the streak to 0.
guard.G10.why.6: With a running total it would be locked here, but the streak is only 2, so the right password gets in.
guard.G10.why.9: Failure 3 in a row, so the account locks now.
guard.G11.brief: Trust a note's address only if it starts with our market address 'https://farm.pi.example/'. Reject look-alike fake addresses. Write the check function.
guard.G11.crowIntro: How about I fool you with an address one letter off~
guard.G11.crowLose: You read addresses to the end? Your eyes are too good!
guard.G11.ria: Read an address to the end. Never trust one just because it looks similar.
guard.G11.title: The Look-Alike Address Note
guard.G11.why.0: It starts exactly like our market address, so trust it.
guard.G11.why.1: It is an order page starting with our market address, so trust it.
guard.G11.why.2: It is http, not https, so reject it.
guard.G11.why.3: Only the start looks similar; it is a different address. Checking through the final / is what blocks it.
guard.G11.why.4: One letter is different (m became n), so it is a fake address.
guard.G11.why.5: Our address appears only in the path; the real address is elsewhere.
guard.G11.why.6: It is a notes page starting with our market address, so trust it.
guard.G12.brief: If an order form contains < > ' characters, it could be used in a web attack, so reject it. Return True if none of them appear, and False if even one does.
guard.G12.crowIntro: Maybe I'll slip a prank character into the order form~
guard.G12.crowLose: Sending an order back over a few characters!
guard.G12.ria: Blocking these three characters is only the first step. The real defense is to swap dangerous characters for safe ones when you print them on screen (escaping).
guard.G12.title: The Order Form With Odd Characters
guard.G12.why.0: There are no dangerous characters, so accept it.
guard.G12.why.1: A comma and an exclamation mark are not dangerous characters, so accept it.
guard.G12.why.2: It contains < and >, so reject it.
guard.G12.why.3: It contains a single quote ('), so reject it.
guard.G12.why.4: Even one > is enough to reject it.
guard.G12.why.5: Parentheses are not dangerous characters, so accept it.
guard.G13.brief: Crow runs a dictionary attack, trying the passwords people use most. Return False for any password on the starter code's common list (upper or lower case does not matter) and True for all others.
guard.G13.crowIntro: Trying them from number one down, one of them has to work~
guard.G13.crowLose: You even made a list? All my favorite passwords are blocked!
guard.G13.ria: Keep a list of obvious passwords and reject them up front. Reject them even when Crow capitalizes them.
guard.G13.title: The Common Password List
guard.G13.why.0: It is not on the common password list, so accept it.
guard.G13.why.1: It is the very first, most common password, so reject it.
guard.G13.why.2: Lowercased it is password, so reject it even in capitals.
guard.G13.why.3: It looks like letmein but nothing on the list matches exactly, so accept it.
guard.G13.why.4: Only the first letter is a capital; it is still qwerty, so reject it.
guard.G13.why.5: It is not on the list, so accept it.
guard.G13.why.6: It is a common password on the list, so reject it.
guard.G13.why.7: A short password that is not on the list is still accepted by this check. Length rules are a separate decision.
guard.G14.brief: This time, instead of writing down bad people, we wrote down who may enter. Return True only if the name is on the starter code's members list, and False for everyone else.
guard.G14.crowIntro: If I keep changing my name, a blocklist can never keep up~
guard.G14.crowLose: Blocking everyone who is not listed? How cold!
guard.G14.ria: A blocklist misses bad names you do not know yet. A list of only the people you let in is safer.
guard.G14.title: Only Guests on the List
guard.G14.why.0: The name is on the list, so let them in.
guard.G14.why.1: The name is not on the list, so reject it.
guard.G14.why.2: The name is on the list, so let them in.
guard.G14.why.3: It looks like pi, but only pi is on the list, so reject it.
guard.G14.why.4: The capital letter makes it different from the name on the list, so reject it.
guard.G14.why.5: An empty name is not on the list, so reject it.
guard.G14.why.6: The last name on the list is let in too.
guard.G15.brief: Crow peeked at one-time entry codes and sends them again. Let in a code the first time it is used and write it in the used list. Block any code already in used.
guard.G15.crowIntro: I'll send the code I peeked at earlier. It's the same one, so what's the harm!
guard.G15.crowLose: A used code is done? Not even recycling?
guard.G15.ria: Write down a one-time code once it is used, and block the same code if it comes again.
guard.G15.title: A Used Code Is Done
guard.G15.why.0: It is a first-time code, so let it in and write it in used.
guard.G15.why.1: It is a first-time code, so let it in and write it in used.
guard.G15.why.2: A1 was already used once, so block it even though it is sent again.
guard.G15.why.3: Lowercase a1 is a different code from A1, so it counts as new and is let in.
guard.G15.why.4: It is a first-time code, so let it in.
guard.G15.why.5: B2 was already used too, so block it.
guard.G15.why.6: C3 was just used, so sending it right away again is blocked too.
guard.G15.why.7: It is a new code, so let it in.
guard.G16.brief: Requests look like 'role:action' (for example owner:delete). Find that role's list of allowed actions in the perms dictionary and return True only if the requested action is in it. An unknown role can do nothing.
guard.G16.crowIntro: I'm a guest, but I'll press the delete button too~
guard.G16.crowLose: Exactly the right permissions for every role? No gaps at all!
guard.G16.ria: Give each role only the permissions it needs. An unknown role gets an empty list and is blocked.
guard.G16.title: What Each Role Can Do
guard.G16.why.0: owner can delete, so let it in.
guard.G16.why.1: guest can read, so let it in.
guard.G16.why.2: guest's list has only read, so write is blocked.
guard.G16.why.3: An unknown role gets an empty list, so even read is blocked.
guard.G16.why.4: farmer can write, so let it in.
guard.G16.why.5: farmer has no delete permission, so block it.
guard.G16.why.6: A capital-O Owner is not a role in the dictionary, so block it.
guard.G16.why.7: It has three parts, so the request is malformed. Do not ignore the extra part and allow it.
guard.G16.why.8: There is no colon, so the action is missing. Block it instead of letting an error happen.
guard.G16.why.9: It has three parts, so the action is not in the second place. Do not allow it by looking only at the last part. The action must be the 2nd of exactly two parts.
guard.G17.brief: Orders arrive one at a time with the sender's address. In the counts dictionary, count each sender's orders: let in up to the 3rd order from the same sender and block the 4th and later.
guard.G17.crowIntro: Sending from just one address will stand out, right? Let me try anyway~
guard.G17.crowLose: Counting per person? You block only me and still accept the other guests!
guard.G17.ria: Block someone who sends too much. Count each person separately in a dictionary.
guard.G17.title: Counting Orders by Sender
guard.G17.why.0: This is crow's 1st order, so let it in.
guard.G17.why.1: This is minji's 1st order, so let it in.
guard.G17.why.2: This is crow's 2nd order, so let it in.
guard.G17.why.3: This is crow's 3rd order, so it is still let in.
guard.G17.why.5: This is minji's 2nd order, so crow's heavy sending does not affect it.
guard.G17.why.6: This is jun's 1st order, so let it in.
guard.G17.why.8: This is minji's 3rd order, so it is let in right up to the limit.
guard.G17.why.9: minji is blocked too once it is the 4th.
guard.G18.brief: Each pass (token) has its minutes left written in the sessions dictionary. Return True only for a pass with at least 1 minute left. A pass not in the dictionary, or one whose time has run out, gets False.
guard.G18.crowIntro: The pass I stole last week must still work, right?
guard.G18.crowLose: Passes expire? Mine is like spoiled milk!
guard.G18.ria: A pass stops working after a while. Treat an unknown pass as having 0 minutes left.
guard.G18.title: The Expired Pass
guard.G18.why.0: It has 30 minutes left, so let it in.
guard.G18.why.1: It has 0 minutes left, an expired pass, so block it.
guard.G18.why.2: Even with just 1 minute left it is still valid, so let it in.
guard.G18.why.3: A pass not in the dictionary counts as 0 minutes left, so block it.
guard.G18.why.4: It has 5 minutes left, so let it in.
guard.G18.why.5: An empty pass is not in the dictionary, so block it.
guard.G19.brief: An app requests permissions joined by commas (for example read,list). Return True only if every requested permission is in the allowed set. If even one is out of range, return False.
guard.G19.crowIntro: I'll say read only, then slip in a request for delete too~
guard.G19.crowLose: Rejecting everything for one extra permission? So stingy!
guard.G19.ria: Check that the requested permissions are a subset of the allowed range. If even one goes over, reject.
guard.G19.title: Are the Requested Permissions in Range?
guard.G19.why.0: read is within the allowed range, so let it in.
guard.G19.why.1: Both permissions are within the allowed range, so let it in.
guard.G19.why.2: delete is out of range, so reject even though only one goes over.
guard.G19.why.4: This request has no allowed permission at all, so reject it.
guard.G19.why.5: Writing the same permission twice leaves just list in the set, so let it in.
guard.G19.why.6: An empty request counts as one empty-text permission, which is out of range, so reject it.
guard.G2.brief: The warehouse is open from 9:00 until before 18:00. Look at the hour someone arrives (0-23) and let them in only during those hours.
guard.G2.concept: Access control: only let in at the set times
guard.G2.crowIntro: Maybe I'll slip in while everyone's asleep~
guard.G2.crowLose: The door won't open at night? Not fair to a night owl like me!
guard.G2.ria: Please keep to the opening hours. Open at exactly 9, close at 18.
guard.G2.title: The Midnight Visitor
guard.G2.why.0: 3 in the morning is outside opening hours.
guard.G2.why.1: Edge case: exactly 9 is open, so let it in.
guard.G2.why.3: 17 is still before closing, so let it in.
guard.G2.why.4: Edge case: from 18 the door is closed.
guard.G20.brief: Requests look like 'place@hour' (for example gate@07, the hour is two characters). Find the place among the (place, start, end) tuples in the rules list and return True only if start <= hour < end. A place not in the list gets False.
guard.G20.crowIntro: I'll lurk in front of the vault in the middle of the night~
guard.G20.crowLose: You memorized the schedule? Poor midnight thieves!
guard.G20.ria: Each place is open at different times. The start hour counts, but the end hour does not. When hours are written as two-digit text, comparing the text gives the same order as comparing numbers — you will learn to turn them into numbers in Chapter 10.
guard.G20.title: Different Hours for Each Place
guard.G20.why.0: Exactly 6 o'clock, the opening hour, is included, so let it in.
guard.G20.why.1: 19 is before the 20 o'clock closing time, so let it in.
guard.G20.why.2: Exactly 20 is the end hour and not included, so block it.
guard.G20.why.3: It is 5 o'clock, before opening, so block it.
guard.G20.why.4: The barn is open from 8 until before 18, so 12 is let in.
guard.G20.why.5: The vault is open only until before 12, so 12 is blocked.
guard.G20.why.6: It is between 9 and 12, when the vault is open, so let it in.
guard.G20.why.7: A place not in rules is blocked.
guard.G21.brief: One account may connect at most 3 devices. Record connected devices in the devices set. Let in a device that is already connected. Let in a new device only if fewer than 3 are connected, and record it. Block anything else.
guard.G21.crowIntro: Let me connect my whole gang's devices to one account~
guard.G21.crowLose: Only three devices? My friends are lining up!
guard.G21.ria: Limiting the number of devices stops account sharing. If the same device comes back, just let it in.
guard.G21.title: Three Devices per Account
guard.G21.why.0: It is the 1st device, so let it in and record it.
guard.G21.why.1: It is the 2nd device, so let it in.
guard.G21.why.2: It is the 3rd device, so let it into the last slot.
guard.G21.why.3: It is already connected, so let it in without using another slot.
guard.G21.why.4: It is a new device, but 3 are already connected, so block it.
guard.G21.why.5: A connected device is let in however many times it comes.
guard.G21.why.6: It is yet another new device, so block it.
guard.G22.brief: Order quantities arrive as text. Return True only for a whole number from 1 to 50. When a non-number makes int() raise an error, the program must not stop; it must return False instead.
guard.G22.crowIntro: What if I type 'one' in the quantity box? Will the shop freeze~
guard.G22.crowLose: It caught the error and kept working? That shop won't fall over!
guard.G22.ria: Bad input must not stop the shop. Wrap the line that might fail in try, and name the exact error.
guard.G22.title: The Quantity That Isn't a Number
guard.G22.why.0: 5 is a whole number from 1 to 50, so let it in.
guard.G22.why.1: 50 is exactly the upper limit, so it still gets in.
guard.G22.why.2: 51 is over the limit, so block it.
guard.G22.why.3: An order of 0 is below 1, so block it.
guard.G22.why.4: int('abc') raises ValueError, but we catch it and block with False.
guard.G22.why.5: An empty text also makes int() raise ValueError, so catch it and block.
guard.G22.why.6: Decimal text makes int() raise ValueError, so block it.
guard.G22.why.7: -4 is negative, below 1, so block it.
guard.G22.why.8: A superscript 2 looks like a digit, but int() cannot read it and raises ValueError, so block it.
guard.G22.why.9: int() ignores the spaces around it and reads 5, an integer from 1 to 50, so let it in.
guard.G23.brief: Bill requests arrive as 'amount/people' (like 30000/3). Return True only if the amount per person is 10000 or less. If the people count is 0 or the shape is wrong and an error occurs, the program must not stop; return False.
guard.G23.crowIntro: If I write 0 people, the calculator will blow up~
guard.G23.crowLose: Zero people or plain letters, it catches it all. Sturdy calculator!
guard.G23.ria: Dividing by 0 raises ZeroDivisionError, and a wrong shape raises ValueError. To catch both, put them in parentheses.
guard.G23.title: The Bill Split by Zero People
guard.G23.why.0: Exactly 10000 per person is within the limit, so let it in.
guard.G23.why.1: 3000 per person, so let it in.
guard.G23.why.2: 15000 per person is over the limit, so block it.
guard.G23.why.3: Dividing by 0 people raises ZeroDivisionError, but we catch it and block.
guard.G23.why.4: There is no '/', so it can't be unpacked; catch the ValueError and block.
guard.G23.why.5: The people count isn't a number, so int() raises ValueError; block it.
guard.G23.why.6: 100 for one person is within the limit, so let it in.
guard.G24.brief: The users dictionary says whether each account is active (True/False). Return True only for an active account. If looking up an account not in the dictionary raises KeyError, the program must not stop; return False (deny) safely.
guard.G24.crowIntro: If I say any name, will you let me in as a stranger~
guard.G24.crowLose: Deny anything unknown? What a thorough doorkeeper!
guard.G24.ria: When something goes wrong, closing the door is safer. By default, an account we don't know does not get in.
guard.G24.title: Unknown Accounts Are Denied by Default
guard.G24.why.0: It is an active account, so let it in.
guard.G24.why.1: It is an active account, so let it in.
guard.G24.why.2: It is in the dictionary but not active, so block it.
guard.G24.why.3: An account not in the dictionary raises KeyError; catch it and deny by default.
guard.G24.why.4: An empty name is not in the dictionary either, so deny by default.
guard.G24.why.5: The capital letters make it a different name, not in the dictionary, so deny it.
guard.G25.brief: The addresses and names to block are in the file blocklist.txt, one per line. Read the file once, and if a request is exactly equal to one of the lines, return False (block); otherwise return True.
guard.G25.concept: Managing the blocklist as a file
guard.G25.crowIntro: If my name is at the bottom of the list, you'll skip right past it~
guard.G25.crowLose: You read every single line? Your eyes are too good!
guard.G25.ria: Keeping the blocklist in a file instead of in code means you can change it by editing the file. Remove the newline at the end of each line with strip().
guard.G25.title: The Blocklist File
guard.G25.why.0: It is on the first line of the list, so block it.
guard.G25.why.1: It is on a middle line of the list, so block it.
guard.G25.why.2: It is on the last line; with the newline removed it matches exactly, so block it.
guard.G25.why.3: It is not on the list, so let the guest in.
guard.G25.why.4: It looks like bot-77, but no line is exactly the same, so let it in.
guard.G25.why.5: An empty request equals none of the lines, so in this case let it in.
guard.G26.brief: The file access.log holds 'user,result' lines (the result is ok or fail). Read the file once and count fails for each user. A user with 3 or more fails gets False (block); anyone with fewer gets True.
guard.G26.crowIntro: If I fail many times and nobody checks the log, nobody will know~
guard.G26.crowLose: You counted everything? My mistakes are written in the ledger!
guard.G26.ria: Records become clues after something happens. Split each line at the comma and count each user's failures in a dictionary.
guard.G26.title: Suspicious Accounts in the Access Log
guard.G26.why.0: It has piled up 4 fails, so block it.
guard.G26.why.1: Exactly 3 fails reaches the limit, so block it.
guard.G26.why.2: Only 2 fails, so it still gets in.
guard.G26.why.3: Mostly ok and only 1 fail, so let it in.
guard.G26.why.4: The log has only ok, so let it in.
guard.G26.why.5: A user not in the log has 0 fails, so let it in.
guard.G27.brief: The file perms.csv is a 'role,write' table (the first line is the header; the write column is yes or no). Use the csv module to read the file once and collect only roles whose write is yes. Return True for those roles and False otherwise.
guard.G27.concept: Managing permissions with a config file
guard.G27.crowIntro: If I slightly change the role name, can I get write permission~
guard.G27.crowLose: Only roles in the table can write? So inflexible!
guard.G27.ria: With permissions in a file, you can change them without editing code. csv.reader gives you a list of cells for each line.
guard.G27.title: The Permissions CSV
guard.G27.why.0: The write column is yes, so let it in.
guard.G27.why.1: The write column is yes, so let it in.
guard.G27.why.2: The write column is no, so block it.
guard.G27.why.3: It is the last line of the table and write is no, so block it.
guard.G27.why.4: A role not in the table is assumed to have no write permission, so block it.
guard.G27.why.5: The capital letter makes it a different role, not in the table, so block it.
guard.G28.brief: The confirmation code must be six digits. Return True only if the whole request text is made of exactly six digits. More or fewer digits, or any other character mixed in, gets False.
guard.G28.crowIntro: If I add one more digit after the code, it will still pass~
guard.G28.crowLose: Exactly six digits only? There isn't a single gap!
guard.G28.ria: Write the allowed shape as a regular expression, then check whether the whole text has that shape. Use fullmatch to check the whole text.
guard.G28.title: The Six-Digit Code
guard.G28.why.0: It is made only of six digits, so let it in.
guard.G28.why.1: Even all zeros are six digits, so let it in.
guard.G28.why.2: Five digits is too few, so block it.
guard.G28.why.3: Seven digits is not the six-digit shape, so block it.
guard.G28.why.4: A non-digit character is mixed in, so block it.
guard.G28.why.5: It has six characters but they are not digits, so block it.
guard.G28.why.6: A space in front means the whole text is not six digits, so block it.
guard.G28.why.7: Empty text has no digits at all, so block it.
guard.G28.why.8: A newline at the end means the whole text is not six digits, so block it.
guard.G28.why.9: These Arabic-Indic digits count as digits for \d, but they are not the 0-9 we accept, so block them.
guard.G29.brief: Find every address (starting with http:// or https://, in any letter case) in the note's text. If the host part (from after :// up to the first /, ?, # or space) of even one is not exactly farm.pi.example, return False (suspected phishing). If there are no addresses, or all are farm.pi.example, return True.
guard.G29.crowIntro: Shall I slip a convincing fake address into the middle of the note~
guard.G29.crowLose: You picked apart every address? My fake link got exposed!
guard.G29.ria: findall returns everything it finds as a list. If the pattern has one pair of parentheses, it collects only the text inside them (the host). First make everything lowercase with lower(), then grab the whole host part and check it is exactly farm.pi.example. With an @ inside, like farm.pi.example@crow.example, the real destination is after the @, so it is not equal and gets blocked.
guard.G29.title: The Note with a Strange Address
guard.G29.why.0: Every address in the note is farm.pi.example, so let it in.
guard.G29.why.1: There is no address at all, so let it in.
guard.G29.why.2: The host is crow.example, a strange address, so block it.
guard.G29.why.3: farm-pi.example is a look-alike fake host, so block it.
guard.G29.why.4: The first address is fine, but the second is strange, so block it.
guard.G29.why.5: It starts with farm.pi.example, but the whole host is somewhere else, so block it.
guard.G29.why.6: The host is pi.example, different from farm.pi.example, so block it.
guard.G29.why.7: What comes before the @ is just decoration; the real destination is crow.example after the @, so block it.
guard.G29.why.8: Even in capital letters, it becomes crow.example once lowercased, so block it.
guard.G3.brief: When taking a new password, refuse the obvious ones (0000, 1234, 1111). The check function should return True for a fine password and False for an obvious one.
guard.G3.ria: Refuse obvious passwords from the start. Please finish the check function.
guard.G3.title: Filtering Obvious Passwords
guard.G3.why.0: It is not obvious, so accept it.
guard.G3.why.1: 0000 is the first one anyone tries.
guard.G3.why.2: 1234 is another obvious password everyone thinks of.
guard.G3.why.3: It is not on the obvious list, so accept it.
guard.G3.why.4: Repeating one digit is an obvious password.
guard.G3.why.5: It is not on the obvious list, so accept it.
guard.G30.brief: A new password must follow all three rules: at least 8 characters, at least one uppercase letter (A-Z), and at least one digit. Break any one and return False; follow all and return True.
guard.G30.crowLose: Uppercase and digits too? Making passwords is hard!
guard.G30.ria: Check the length with len, and look for an uppercase letter and a digit with re.search. Send it back as soon as one rule is broken.
guard.G30.title: Password Policy
guard.G30.why.0: Exactly 8 characters with an uppercase letter and a digit, so let it in.
guard.G30.why.1: 7 characters is too short, so block it.
guard.G30.why.2: There is no uppercase letter, so block it.
guard.G30.why.3: There is no digit, so block it.
guard.G30.why.4: The length and digits are fine, but there is no uppercase letter, so block it.
guard.G30.why.5: Length, uppercase and digit are all satisfied, so let it in.
guard.G30.why.6: An empty password is too short from the start, so block it.
guard.G31.brief: Return True only if the address starts with https and its host is exactly farm.pi.example. Look-alike hosts, http addresses, or addresses with something stuck around the host are False. A port number (like :443) is not part of the host, so ignore it. If the address contains a \, return False.
guard.G31.concept: Domain check (read an address by its parts)
guard.G31.crowIntro: If I slip farm.pi.example into the address, you'll be fooled~
guard.G31.crowLose: You read the address part by part? My fake address got exposed!
guard.G31.ria: Use urlparse to split an address into parts (scheme, hostname, port, path). It is far more exact than looking only at the start of the text.
guard.G31.title: Read the Address to the End
guard.G31.why.0: It is https and the host is farm.pi.example, so let it in.
guard.G31.why.1: Even with a port number the host is farm.pi.example, so let it in.
guard.G31.why.2: It is http, not https, so block it.
guard.G31.why.3: Only the start looks alike; the real host is on evil.example, so block it.
guard.G31.why.4: farm.pi.example is only in the path; the host is evil.example, so block it.
guard.G31.why.5: What comes before @ is a user name; the real host is evil.example, so block it.
guard.G31.why.6: There is no https://, so the scheme is empty. Block it.
guard.G31.why.7: An empty address has no scheme and no host, so block it.

guard.G33.brief: Find every href="..." and src="..." link in the note (HTML text). A link is fine only if it is an http or https link whose host is farm.pi.example, or it is a link inside the site (like /notes/7). A link inside the site has no scheme (the front part like https: or javascript:) and no host, and starts with / but not //. A link that contains a \ anywhere is not fine either. Return False if there is even one link that is not fine, otherwise True. Look for links in both href and src attributes, with double quotes and single quotes, and ignore the case of the attribute name and any spaces around =. If a link contains &, treat it as not fine (a character reference like / is read by the browser as another character).

A javascript: link runs code the moment it is clicked, and browsers read //evil.example or /\evil.example as an outside host. So let in only the 'safe shapes'. Reading even attributes written without quotes, like href=/x, takes a real HTML parser, and so does anything beyond href and src, like action on a form. A character reference like / is read by the browser as a slash, so a link with & is blocked. Other attributes and other hidden spellings need a real parser, so here we handle only quoted href and src.

guard.G7.why.1: Ria has permission too, so let her in.
guard.G7.why.2: A guest has no key permission, even if verified.
guard.G7.why.3: A courier is not a role that uses the warehouse key.
guard.G7.why.4: A different capital letter means a different role name, so block it.
guard.G7.why.5: Crow is not a role with permission.
guard.G7.why.6: The owner gets in every time.
guard.G7.why.7: It is only the beginning of owner, not the whole role name, so block it.
guard.G7.why.8: It is owner with extra characters, a different role name, so block it.
guard.G7.why.9: An empty value is not any role, so block it.
guard.G8.brief: New name tags must be 1 to 12 characters. Reject empty or too-long tags. The check function returns True to accept and False to reject.
guard.G8.crowIntro: How about I write a whole novel on the tag~
guard.G8.crowLose: Only twelve letters? My story got cut off!
guard.G8.ria: Check the length of an input first. Reject it if it is too short or too long.
guard.G8.title: The Name Tag That Is Too Long
guard.G8.why.0: 2 characters is within the limit, so accept it.
guard.G8.why.1: 9 characters is within the limit, so accept it.
guard.G8.why.3: An empty value can't be a name tag, so reject it.
guard.G8.why.4: Boundary: from 13 characters it is too long, so reject it.
guard.G8.why.5: 40 characters is far too long, so reject it.
guard.G8.why.6: Boundary: even 1 character is accepted as a tag.
guard.G9.brief: A one-time confirmation code sent by text works for only 5 minutes after it is made. Each attempt is the number of minutes since the code was made (an integer). Return True within 5 minutes and False after.
guard.G9.crowIntro: Yesterday's confirmation code should still work~
guard.G9.crowLose: Already expired? I didn't know codes go bad!
guard.G9.ria: Old codes are risky. Please make codes unusable after 5 minutes.
guard.G9.title: The Expired Confirmation Code
guard.G9.why.0: A brand-new code, so it works.
guard.G9.why.1: 3 minutes have passed, so it is still within 5.
guard.G9.why.3: Boundary: past 5 minutes it has expired.
guard.G9.why.4: A code 30 minutes old has expired.
guard.G9.why.5: A code a day old expired long ago.
